Assembly of SCARA Robot Mechanism Assembly of the alpha prototype is shown in Figure 12. The robot arm is assembled and connected to the vertical ball-screw mechanism in the base. The ball-screw motor and “shoulder” motor are installed, along with assembly of the elbow, wrist and nozzle. Controls improvements were made leading to the first successful trials of the robot. These improvements included a new location for the vision camera. An extension was added to the end effector to mount the camera behind and below the nozzle, affording a better overall field of view (Figure 14). Page 15 of 31 This device includes two cameras, a 1920 x 1080 @ 30Hz color video camera and a 1024 x 768 @ 30Hz lidar. The lidar uses a single near-infrared (NIR) laser beam, swept over the field of view (FOV) using a micro-electromechanical system (MEMS). The lidar’s output consists of a depth map and a NIR image. Ambient light affects the two cameras in opposite ways. The color camera requires at least some light to operate, but it can handle full sunlight. The lidar is its own light source and can therefore operate in complete darkness, but it gets overpowered by sunlight. Marker detection can be done using either the color or NIR image, but accurate 3D pose and yaw estimation requires the depth map. A stereo camera could also be used, since it produces both an image (color or monochrome) and a depth map. In our experimentation so far, depth accuracy was somewhat better using lidar than a stereo camera. Size and placement of the ArUco markers was optimized to improve performance. The design for this project included a pair of 4.2 cm markers (on a 5.6 cm sticker, since the marker’s black edge needs a surrounding white border). As shown in Figure 15, the markers are placed near the left and right edges of the fuel cell, just below the receptacle. The left marker provides both 3D pose and yaw, while the right marker provides additional accuracy in yaw. Pose estimation require a precise calibration of the distance from the left marker’s center to the receptacle’s center (whereas the right marker just needs to be roughly aligned with the left one). Having two markers also enables a much larger number of uniquely identifiable fuel cells. The largest ArUco dictionary has 1,000 unique IDs, which is potentially not enough for one site. Using a pair of markers provides 1,000 x 1,000 = 1 million unique permutations. Figure 15: ArUco marker placement The OpenCV marker detection code provides the image coordinate
